transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-03-25
Start Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Avery Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Alvarez (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Orchid CTO), Daniel Park (Orchid ML Eng), Liam O'Connor (Orchid Infra)

Summary:
Quick technical deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy for Orchid's multi-tenant assistant product. Covered cache key design, hit-rate expectations, eviction and TTL strategies, multi-tenant safety and encryption, warmup and prefetch, quantization impact on cacheability, batching and latency tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed next steps to run benchmarks and exchange sample prompt sets and security docs.

Topics:
- Cache key construction and hashing
- Tenant isolation and multi-tenant safety
- Hit-rate modeling and benchmarks
- Eviction policies, TTL, and stale reads
- Batch sizing and tail latency impacts
- Quantization + KV cache compatibility
- VPC/on-prem encryption and KMS integration

Transcript:
[00:00] Avery Chen: All right hey everyone thanks for making time today. quick intro, I'm Avery on the AE side, Marco's our SE, um we'll focus on prefix caching strategy for your assistant use case. Priya do you wanna kick off with goals?
[00:30] Priya Singh: Sure, thanks Avery. Um main rubric is latency < 120ms tail for chat, cost reduction target 40% from baseline. Also we need strict tenant isolation, and we run in a VPC for now, potential on-prem next quarter.
[01:00] Marco Alvarez: Got it. For context, prefix caching means we store the KV state for common prefixes so that we don't recompute attention for the same prompt starts. can save a lot on LLM token compute if hit rate's high.
[01:30] Daniel Park: Quick question — our prompts are templated and have variable user slots, e.g., "Summarize the following conversation between A and B" plus blob. How do you identify the portion to cache?
[02:00] Marco Alvarez: Good question. Two main approaches: 1) deterministic template separation: treat the static prompt head as the prefix key; 2) fingerprinting: hash the normalized prompt (strip names, slot placeholders) to get keys. both have tradeoffs — template-based is simpler and explainable, fingerprinting can be more flexible but harder to debug.
[02:30] Priya Singh: We have ~120 templates currently; some have optional sections that vary. Is there an approach for optional blocks?
[03:00] Marco Alvarez: We typically normalize optional blocks into canonical representations before hashing. e.g., collapse optional section markers, or create multiple canonical variants. But note explosion risk — combinatorial templates lower hit rate unless you canonicalize aggressively.
[03:30] Liam O'Connor: What about eviction? If we keep millions of prefixes in the KV cache, memory mounting could be an issue on dedicated nodes.
[04:00] Marco Alvarez: Yes, eviction strategy is critical. We recommend a size-tiered LRU with per-tenant caps. Also consider time-based TTLs for low-frequency prefixes; for heavy hitters use pinning. Redwood Dedicated allows per-customer memory quotas so one tenant doesn't evict everyone else.
[04:30] Daniel Park: Any specifics on hit-rate expectations? ballpark numbers?
[05:00] Marco Alvarez: Depends on your template reuse. For templated chat with 120 templates, if templates account for 60% of token cost, and variable slots are small, you could see 30-60% effective token savings. But that's optimistic; baseline benchmark is needed. We'll run a sim.
[05:30] Priya Singh: When you say "token savings" — that maps to lower GPU time and latency right?
[06:00] Marco Alvarez: Correct. If prefix KV is hit we avoid the first N attention steps compute. For long prefixes this can significantly reduce latency and cost. But be mindful of small prefixes where batching/overhead may dominate.
[06:30] Avery Chen: Let's talk keys — what should the cache key include? tenant id, template id, normalized prompt head, model name, model revision, quantization profile?
[07:00] Marco Alvarez: Exactly. We suggest a stable key: hash(tenant_id || template_id || normalized_prefix || model_id || model_revision || quant_profile). Include sequence-length bucket and truncation policy if you vary max context. This ensures correctness (you never serve wrong KV for different model params).
[07:30] Daniel Park: Is the quant_profile necessary? if we quantize binary artifacts differ, right?
[08:00] Marco Alvarez: Yes, quantization changes kernel behavior and possibly cache layout. In some optimized runtimes the KV format differs by quantization and kernel set, so treating quant_profile as part of key avoids subtle mismatches.
[08:30] Priya Singh: How do you handle multi-tenant safety? We're worried about one tenant's data being cached and accidentally served to another.
[09:00] Marco Alvarez: Per-tenant keys are mandatory. We also support per-tenant encryption at rest. For shared caches we keep tenant namespace isolation via key prefixes and enforce ACLs. On Dedicated or Private deployments you can opt for physical isolation too.
[09:30] Liam O'Connor: For Private/on-prem we have a HSM and KMS — how will that integrate?
[10:00] Marco Alvarez: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. Cache blobs can be encrypted with tenant keys; metadata stays in control plane. For fully air-gapped installs we provide offline key rotation procedures. We'll share the securitywhitepaper.
[10:30] Avery Chen: Note for the record we'll attach SOC2 and the KMS integration notes in the follow up.
[11:00] Daniel Park: On TTLs — do you recommend short TTLs to avoid stale knowledge, or longer TTLs to maximize hits?
[11:30] Marco Alvarez: It depends on your tolerance for staleness. For dynamic prefix content (e.g., system prompts that update) use short TTLs or versioned keys. For stable templates you can use long TTLs and explicit invalidation when you roll a template change. We recommend versioning the template id in the key for safe rollouts.
[12:00] Priya Singh: If we version templates frequently, will that blow up the cache size?
[12:30] Marco Alvarez: It can. Best practice: use canary rollout with small percentage pinned to new templates, and only warm the cache for new templates progressively. Also retire old keys after an appropriate TTL.
[13:00] Avery Chen: Let's discuss warmup and prefetch — can Redwood pre-warm KV for a rollout?
[13:30] Marco Alvarez: Yes, we have APIs to prepopulate cache for specific keys. For example, before full release you can pre-warm the heavy hitter prefixes using a bulk job. That reduces initial cold-start tail.
[14:00] Daniel Park: On metrics — what should we measure to understand the impact?
[14:30] Marco Alvarez: Hit rate by template, tokens saved, tail latency (p95/p99), CPU/GPU utilization, and cost delta. Also track cache churn and eviction rates per tenant. We'll provide dashboards in Redwood Console.
[15:00] Priya Singh: Another tangent — batching interactions with cached prefixes, any gotchas?
[15:30] Marco Alvarez: Yes, batching can interact poorly with cache hits if you rely on variable prefix lengths. For example if one request needs a 50-token prefix and another 10-token, the KV reuse may be limited. Continuous batching logic in our runtime groups by compatible context lengths and model kernel selection to maximize both batching and prefix reuse. But the runtime has to be configured correctly — batch windowing and grouping heuristics matter.
[16:00] Daniel Park: So we'd want similar sequence length distribution to benefit both batching and cache hit?
[16:30] Marco Alvarez: Exactly. We can analyze your traffic distribution and recommend batch/window settings.
[17:00] Priya Singh: Quantization — we plan to serve q4_8 and q5_0 profiles for cost. Any limitations on caching across quant profiles?
[17:30] Marco Alvarez: Cache blobs are not interchangeable across quant profiles; include quant_profile in key. Also some optimizations (like KV packing) differ, so double-check compatibility. In practice we store separate caches per quant profile or use unified metadata mapping keys to profile-specific blobs.
[18:00] Avery Chen: Let's surface a realistic simulation plan — Marco, can you outline the benchmark you'll run?
[18:30] Marco Alvarez: We'll take the five template families you give, synthesize a trace with slot variability matching your distribution, run 24-hour simulated QPS with the target mix, and measure hit rates across templates, p95/p99 latency improvement, and memory footprint for the cache. We'll run under both q4_8 and q5_0 quant profiles, and with and without pre-warm.
[19:00] Daniel Park: Will that emulate our VPC latency and dedicated throughput?
[19:30] Marco Alvarez: We'll emulate compute characteristics; for network/disk differences in VPC/on-prem we might need telemetry from your infra. For Dedicated we can provision a similar node shape.
[20:00] Priya Singh: Any thoughts on cache-key size and hashing collision risk?
[20:30] Marco Alvarez: Use a 256-bit hash (e.g., SHA-256) and store the full canonical string in metadata for debugging. Collisions are astronomically unlikely, but metadata helps trace issues. Also include a short human-readable suffix for ops debugging.
[21:00] Liam O'Connor: Could a tenant DoS us by generating many unique prefixes to thrash cache?
[21:30] Marco Alvarez: That's why per-tenant caps and write-rate quotas exist. You can also enable adaptive rate-limiting and auto-eviction policies to protect shared nodes. In Dedicated you can isolate high-cardinality tenants to separate pools.
[22:00] Priya Singh: How does Redwood handle serialized KV formats across runtime updates — will an upgrade invalidate caches?
[22:30] Marco Alvarez: We version cache blobs by runtime revision as part of the key. When the runtime changes in an incompatible way we either migrate blobs or start a fresh cache. We try to minimize incompatible changes and provide rolling compatibility paths.
[23:00] Daniel Park: Are there monitoring hooks for cache-debugging? e.g., show top-N keys, last-access times, per-tenant memory usage?
[23:30] Marco Alvarez: Yes, Redwood Console exposes per-route cache metrics, top hot keys, eviction histograms, and per-tenant quotas. We can add custom logs for debugging under SE support.
[24:00] Priya Singh: On the legal side, if cached prefixes contain user PII accidentally, do you support redaction before caching?
[24:30] Marco Alvarez: Redwood can implement normalization/redaction hooks pre-cache. Best practice is to canonicalize and remove PII before caching. For sensitive data you can opt-out of caching altogether per route.
[25:00] Priya Singh: That would be important for regulatory reasons.
[25:30] Avery Chen: OK let's talk numbers again — what memory footprint per prefix?
[26:00] Marco Alvarez: It varies by model and prefix length. Rough order: small prefix (256 tokens) KV blob maybe tens to low hundreds of KB after compression; longer prefixes grow linearly. We'll give a more precise estimate after Marco's sim with your representative prompts.
[26:30] Daniel Park: For our expected 1000 QPS steady state, any concerns about eviction churn?
[27:00] Marco Alvarez: If your access pattern has high cardinality, yes. We'll model churn in the sim; also recommend warming hot keys and limiting cache writes for ephemeral prefixes.
[27:30] Priya Singh: One more — what about cross-tenant dedup? If two tenants happen to use identical template text, can we dedup to save memory?
[28:00] Marco Alvarez: We avoid cross-tenant sharing by default for safety. If you're comfortable with shared dedup you can opt-in and use sanitized shared caches. But default is strict namespace separation.
[28:30] Liam O'Connor: For on-prem, do we get the same console visibility?
[29:00] Marco Alvarez: Private deployments include a console agent that ships metrics to your observability stack or optionally to Redwood Console in a controlled way. We can adapt to your policies.
[29:30] Daniel Park: What's the overhead of checking the cache itself on request path? does GET-add latency offset savings for small prefixes?
[30:00] Marco Alvarez: Cache lookup is optimized and adds very low latency (single-digit ms) on local memory caches. For networked or disk-backed caches it's higher. There's a sweet spot where small prefixes may not be worth caching; we measure that in the sim and recommend per-template thresholds.
[30:30] Priya Singh: Any best practices for template design to maximize hit-rate?
[31:00] Marco Alvarez: Keep common phrasing at the head, normalize variable slots, avoid ad-hoc optional sentences, and prefer explicit template ids so you can control cache keys and versioning.
[31:30] Avery Chen: Let's touch on invalidation patterns — what's pragmatic?
[32:00] Marco Alvarez: Use versioned template ids for schema-level changes, use TTL for soft invalidation, and provide an explicit purge API for rollouts or emergency fixes. Avoid ad-hoc edits without version bumps.
[32:30] Daniel Park: For analytics, how do we attribute cost savings to prefix caching?
[33:00] Marco Alvarez: We produce pre/post roll figures: tokens avoided, GPU-hours saved, and cost delta. Redwood Console can attribute per-route savings and show ROI over time.
[33:30] Priya Singh: Any gotchas with third-party dependencies like transformers vs. trimmed kernels?
[34:00] Marco Alvarez: Kernel selection matters: some optimized runtimes change the shape of KV caching and how efficient prefix reuse is. We'll recommend specific runtime builds and kernel flags for your model family.
[34:30] Daniel Park: Does Redwood support mixed-precision ops that affect cache determinism?
[35:00] Marco Alvarez: Mixed precision is fine as long as it's stable across runs; but again include precision profile in cache keys. Determinism concerns are mostly around alignment of runtime and model variant.
[35:30] Priya Singh: About security — will our tenants' cached blobs be encrypted in memory?
[36:00] Marco Alvarez: In-memory encryption is possible but has performance implications; generally we encrypt at-rest and rely on OS-level protections for memory. For high-security customers we can discuss enclave-like approaches or tenant-dedicated nodes.
[36:30] Liam O'Connor: What does the migration path look like if we move from Hosted to Dedicated or On-Prem?
[37:00] Marco Alvarez: We can export/import cache blobs with provenance metadata; but often a re-warm is simpler. We'll provide tools to migrate heavy hitters.
[37:30] Priya Singh: Are there known regression risks when enabling prefix caching?
[38:00] Marco Alvarez: Behaviorally you should be equivalent, but watch for subtle differences around system prompt changes and hidden state assumptions. Always run A/B tests and evals on prompt sets. Redwood's rollout tooling supports canarying and automatic rollback on quality regression alerts.
[38:30] Avery Chen: Speaking of evals — we'll tie quality checks to your eval prompts so we catch regressions.
[39:00] Daniel Park: For the simulation, include p95/p99 and cost, and also track any cases where cached prefixes caused quality degradations.
[39:30] Marco Alvarez: Will do. We'll include confusion matrices for a sampled set.
[40:00] Priya Singh: If we do pre-warm, how do we prevent stale cache after a template edit?
[40:30] Marco Alvarez: Pre-warm should be coupled with either versioned keys or an immediate purge of old blobs as part of the deployment process.
[41:00] Liam O'Connor: Any recommended tooling from Redwood to visualize per-tenant cache usage?
[41:30] Marco Alvarez: Redwood Console has per-tenant memory heatmaps, top keys, and eviction counters. We'll share a screenshot mockup in the follow-up.
[42:00] Priya Singh: On the legal/PII point — we'll likely request a policy that certain prompt classes cannot be cached. Do you support route-level cache disable?
[42:30] Marco Alvarez: Yes, route-level or template-level cache disable is supported. You can also set explicit redaction hooks.
[43:00] Daniel Park: For the benchmark, can we include traffic spikes to test tail behavior?
[43:30] Marco Alvarez: Absolutely — we'll simulate steady-state and spike loads and measure tail latencies and cold-start behavior.
[44:00] Priya Singh: How do we monitor for cache poisoning or tampering?
[44:30] Marco Alvarez: Audit logs and signed cache metadata help. We also have integrity checks and HMACs on cache blobs for Private deployments. We'll include these in the security notes.
[45:00] Avery Chen: Are there examples of customers who saw major wins with prefix caching?
[45:30] Marco Alvarez: Yes, a few conversational SaaS customers saw 30-50% token compute reduction and 2x improvement in tail latency for templated flows. We'll anonymize case studies and share.
[46:00] Priya Singh: Good. One quick operational question — how long to provision Dedicated nodes for doing a controlled pilot?
[46:30] Marco Alvarez: Typically 2-3 weeks to stand up and tune, faster if we reuse existing infra. For Private on-prem, depends on your procurement but the software side is quick.
[47:00] Daniel Park: Any final implementation caveats?
[47:30] Marco Alvarez: Watch for high-cardinality dynamic prefixes, prefer canonicalization, include model and quant metadata in keys, use per-tenant caps, and run sim benchmarks.
[48:00] Priya Singh: Sounds good. Let's recap next steps.
[48:30] Avery Chen: Recap: Redwood sends design doc and security whitepaper; Orchid shares prompt families and traffic distribution; Redwood runs sim and returns benchmark; schedule follow-up week of 2026-04-13.
[49:00] Priya Singh: Confirmed. We'll get the prompt families together by Monday.
[49:30] Daniel Park: Thanks everyone.
[50:00] Marco Alvarez: Thanks — we'll get started on the sim and loop back.
[50:30] Avery Chen: Appreciate it, we'll follow up with links and the doc. Bye all.
[51:00] Priya Singh: Bye.
[51:30] (call ends)
